title: Emergency Business Funding: What to Do When Cash Runs Short
seo_title: Emergency Business Funding: Fast Options | Fidelity Funding
meta_description: Emergency business funding for sudden repairs, lost revenue or unexpected bills: fast options, trade-offs, and how to avoid panic decisions.
dek: A flood, a failed compressor, a lost client: when cash is needed now, a clear head about options protects you from a costly mistake.
intro: The call comes at 6 a.m.: a pipe burst overnight and the shop is under two inches of water. Or your biggest customer just announced they will pay in 90 days instead of 30, and payroll is Friday. Emergencies rarely wait for a perfect loan application.

That urgency is exactly when business owners are most likely to accept the first offer, whatever it costs. Fast funding exists and can be genuinely useful, but speed is the most expensive feature in finance, and a few minutes of structure can save you thousands.
This guide sorts emergencies into types, shows the options that move quickly, and offers a simple framework for deciding without panicking.

paragraphs: Not every emergency needs the same solution. A one-time repair is a bounded cost with a clear end. A revenue shock, like a lost contract or a slow season arriving early, is a recurring gap that may last months. A timing problem, where money is owed to you but not yet received, is different again. Naming which one you face determines whether a short loan, a line of credit, invoice factoring or a longer-term solution makes sense.
bullets: Bounded cost: equipment failure, storm damage, a surprise tax or compliance bill
Revenue drop: lost client, closure, supply disruption
Timing gap: slow-paying customers, delayed insurance claim, pending reimbursement

paragraphs: Several products are built for speed, and they differ in cost and structure. Short-term loans deliver a lump sum with a fixed payment schedule. A merchant cash advance repays from a share of future receipts. Invoice factoring turns unpaid invoices into cash. A business line of credit, if you already have one, is usually the cheapest emergency tool because there is nothing new to apply for. Equipment financing may cover a replacement machine directly.

Funding partners available through a broker depend on your profile, and decisions are often made within hours, with funding often within about a day once approved. That is never guaranteed, and missing documents are the most common cause of delay.

Say a bakery's walk-in cooler dies and replacement plus installation is $14,000. Waiting a week risks spoiled inventory and lost orders. The owner compares a short-term loan with a total payback of $16,800 over 20 weeks, roughly $840 weekly, with an equipment financing offer of $15,500 over 36 months, about $430 monthly. The first is quicker; the second is cheaper overall but may take a bit longer. Neither answer is universally right. What matters is that the owner sees both numbers before choosing. These figures are hypothetical.
Pressure leads to predictable mistakes. Resist them with a short checklist before you sign anything.
steps: Write down the exact amount you need and by when. Do not borrow for the dream scenario.
Ask for the total payback in dollars, the payment frequency, and every fee deducted from the proceeds.
Test the payment against your slowest recent week of deposits.
Check for early-payoff terms, personal guarantees and any lien on business assets.
Compare at least two options, even if it takes an extra hour.

sections.h2: Red flags when you are in a hurry
paragraphs: Be wary of anyone who pressures you to sign immediately, refuses to put terms in writing, asks for large upfront fees before funding, or cannot explain the total cost. Stacking multiple fast advances on top of each other is another trap, since the combined daily payments can drain the account faster than the emergency itself. A legitimate partner will explain the contract and give you time to read it.

Documentation is the part you control. Keep the last several months of business bank statements, a government ID, your business formation details and a voided check in a folder you can send in minutes. If the emergency involves a quote or invoice, such as a repair estimate, include it. Responding quickly to follow-up questions is often what separates a same-day decision from a stalled file, so stay reachable and ask what the partner still needs.

sections.h2: Non-borrowing moves to pair with funding
paragraphs: Borrowing is not the only lever. Call your landlord, suppliers and utilities and ask about payment plans. Check your insurance policy for coverage you may have forgotten. Offer customers a discount for early payment. Delay non-essential spending. These steps can reduce how much you need to borrow, which reduces cost.
Once the dust settles, consider building a reserve so the next emergency does not require a rush decision.

After the crisis is stabilized, do a short review. Ask what could have signaled the problem earlier, whether insurance would have covered part of it, and how much of a cash buffer would have prevented the scramble. Even a modest reserve, built gradually, can mean the next emergency is an inconvenience rather than a panic. If you used a daily-payment product, set a calendar reminder to review the balance and ask about renewals only when you truly need them.

Fidelity Funding is a broker that connects you with funding partners, so one short application can surface several structures instead of one pressured quote. The initial review uses a soft credit pull, and a funding specialist walks through payments and total cost with you. If time matters, tell the specialist your deadline, have recent bank statements ready, and start the application.

key_takeaways: Classify the emergency: bounded cost, revenue drop, or timing gap.
Fast funding costs more; always compare total payback, not just speed.
Test the payment against your slowest week before signing.
Combine borrowing with practical moves like payment plans and early-pay discounts.

faq.q: How fast can emergency business funding arrive?
faq.a: Some funding partners decide within hours and fund within about a day after approval, but timing is never guaranteed. Complete documents, recent bank statements and an available business account speed things up. Tell your specialist about the deadline. If you are unsure, ask for the details in writing and compare them side by side before deciding. A funding specialist can show you what each structure would cost in total dollars, which is often more useful than speed alone.

faq.q: Can I get emergency funding with bad credit?
faq.a: Possibly. Several fast products weigh bank deposits and time in business more than credit score, though costs may be higher with weaker credit. Options vary by partner and profile, and approval is not guaranteed. Your specific situation, documents and bank activity will shape what is actually offered to you. Higher cost is common with weaker credit, so a smaller amount or shorter term may reduce the total you pay.

faq.q: What is the cheapest emergency option?
faq.a: Usually an existing line of credit, followed by equipment financing for asset replacements. Faster products tend to cost more. The best choice depends on how quickly you need money and what you qualify for. A short conversation with a funding specialist can clarify which option realistically fits your profile. If the emergency is a repair, ask whether equipment financing or a payment plan from the vendor could be less expensive than a general cash product.

faq.q: Should I use a personal credit card?
faq.a: It can work for small amounts if you can repay quickly, but it mixes personal and business finances and may carry high interest. Compare it against business funding options and consult an accountant for your situation. Reviewing the full contract, and a CPA or attorney where appropriate, is always a sensible step. Credit cards can bridge a few days but are best treated as a stopgap; a short consultation with your accountant can help.

faq.q: What if I am already repaying another advance?
faq.a: Additional obligations increase daily or weekly payment burden. Disclose existing debts honestly, since partners will see them in bank statements. A specialist can discuss consolidation or lower-payment structures rather than stacking another payment. Every business is different, so a funding specialist can walk through how this applies to your numbers. If the payments are already tight, sharing that openly lets a specialist look for lower-payment structures instead of another fast stack.
